newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Thousands demand return to Communism in Ukraine.
newsitem.headline: Thousands demand return to Communism in Ukraine.

text.p: Tens of thousands of people across Ukraine demanded a return to Communist power on Tuesday during a leftist "Day of Action" protesting against unpaid wages.
"Wages, wages," chanted a crowd of about 3,000 mostly elderly people in old coats and worn-out shoes as they marched under the Red Flag past parliament and the main government building in Kiev.
They waved their fists at deputies who watched through windows as police kept the crowd at a distance.

Ukraine's backlog of unpaid wages and pensions was put at 4.2 billion hryvnia ($2.3 billion) by President Leonid Kuchma last week. It is still growing because parliament has yet to pass a 1997 budget.

The crowd carried an effigy of a businessman hanging upside down with U.S. dollars falling from his pockets -- an expression of resentment against the nouveau riche, dollar-bearing class which has emerged since independence in 1991.
Some 5,000 Communist supporters demonstrated for wages in Dnipropetrovsk, Kuchma's eastern industrial hometown.
Many others stood outside the Yuzhmash missile plant he headed before being elected president in 1994.
Interior Minister Yuri Kravchenko was quoted by Interfax-Ukraine news agency as saying up to 85,000 people took part in protests in the country of 51 million.
"Power to the communists!" a crowd of about 3,500 chanted in the southern Crimean city of Simferopol, waving banners with slogans like: "The motherland is calling you back to the USSR".

Left-wing groups had tried to organise a nationwide strike and communist deputies quit the chamber in Kiev to protest the backlog, which many blame on tight monetary policies advocated by the International Monetary Fund.
But a mining official in Donetsk, centre of the eastern coal region, told Reuters by telephone that about eight of 250 pits were on strike -- "about the same number as usual".
Some 7,000 protestors in Donetsk said they would start a petition for Kuchma's resignation unless he brought order to the country by May 1 -- International Labour Day.
Elsewhere smaller crowds gathered in the streets to register their protest at average monthly wages of $80 to $90, pensions of $30 and price growth of almost 40 percent last year.

In the western city of Lviv, a bastion of Ukrainian nationalism, about 200 communists faced off an equal number of nationalists, who yelled "Pack your suitcases and go back to Russia." Police kept them apart.
A nationalist rally in Kiev earlier in the day attracted about 500 people who broadly back Kuchma and reforms.
"Communist pigs! Filth!" yelled one elderly woman, giving voice to hatred for the memory of the Soviet-era communist party whose successor has formed the biggest group in parliament.
Some of the crowd from the Rukh nationalist party, which spearheaded Ukraine's independence drive in 1991, blew whistles and played the national anthem on flutes.
They blamed the non-payments on the fact that so many members of Ukraine's industrialist class are former communists.
"In Ukraine 80 percent of the factory bosses are communists. They're the ones who are not paying wages. They've re-painted themselves. They're still communists underneath," he said.
The crowds in Simferopol were boosted by pro-Moscow sentiment in the Crimean Peninsula, where 75 percent of the people are ethnic Russians and many want a return to Kremlin rule.
"Kuchma! Don't scare us with NATO! We want a union with our Russian brother!" one banner read.
Ukraine has not ruled out seeking entry to the Western military alliance in future but the communists were more interested in joining forces with like-minded kin in Russia.
